chapter.title: Furniture; bedding, mattresses, mattress supports, cushions and similar stuffed furnishings; luminaires and lighting fittings, not elsewhere specified or included; illuminated signs, illuminated nameplates and the like; prefabricated buildings

page.h1: HTS Chapter 94: Furniture; bedding, mattresses, mattress supports, cushions and similar stuffed furnishings; luminaires and lighting fittings, not elsewhere specified or included; illuminated signs, illuminated nameplates and the like; prefabricated buildings — U.S. Export Rules & Ways to Pay Less Abroad

seo.title: Furniture HS Codes & Export Rules: Schedule B, Licences, CPSC
seo.shortDescription: HS and Schedule B codes for chairs, sofas, furniture parts, mattresses and LED fixtures, plus what the U.S. requires before export: licences, CPSC notices, AES.

intro: Exporting furniture, seats, mattresses or lighting from the U.S. takes little federal paperwork: find the Schedule B number, screen the buyer and file in AES (shipments to Canada are generally exempt). Almost all Chapter 94 goods are **EAR99**, so no Commerce licence is needed except for sanctioned destinations: **Russia and Belarus** need a BIS licence for aircraft and motor-vehicle seats, wooden office furniture and prefabricated buildings, and aircraft seats can be civil-aircraft parts under **ECCN 9A991.d**. Two agency rules matter: a product that does not meet U.S. **CPSC** rules (such as a mattress that fails the federal flammability standards) can be exported only after a notice to CPSC **30 days** ahead, and hospital beds and other **medical furniture** are FDA-regulated devices, for which FDA issues the export certificates foreign regulators ask for.

steps.title: Find the Schedule B number
steps.whatToDo: Look up the 10-digit Schedule B number for each product with the Census Bureau's free search tool. Its first six digits are the same as the HS code every country uses, so it also tells you which line of the buyer's tariff applies. The U.S. import (HTS) number and the Schedule B number match only to six digits.
steps.when: Every export. It goes on the export filing (the last step) and on the commercial invoice.
steps.chapterNote: Seats are 9401: office swivel chairs 9401.39 (9401.31 if of wood), upholstered wooden-frame sofas and chairs 9401.61, upholstered metal-frame seats 9401.71, motor-vehicle seats 9401.20, aircraft seats 9401.10 and seat parts 9401.91 (wood) or 9401.99 (other, the largest U.S. export line). Furniture is 9403: metal office furniture 9403.10, other metal 9403.20, wooden office, kitchen, bedroom and other furniture 9403.30–9403.60, plastic 9403.70, parts 9403.91 (wood) and 9403.99 (other). Medical furniture and its parts are 9402, mattress supports 9404.10, mattresses 9404.21 and 9404.29, LED chandeliers and ceiling and wall fittings 9405.11, LED table, desk and floor lamps 9405.21, other LED luminaires 9405.42, lamp parts 9405.91 (glass), 9405.92 (plastic) and 9405.99 (other) and prefabricated buildings 9406.10 (wood), 9406.20 (steel modular units) and 9406.90 (other). The first six digits of the 10-digit Schedule B number are the HS code on the Overview.

steps.title: Screen the buyer and everyone in the deal
steps.whatToDo: Check the buyer, the end user and any agent against the Consolidated Screening List. It combines the Commerce lists (Entity List, Denied Persons, Unverified, Military End-User), the State Department lists and the Treasury (OFAC) sanctions lists of parties you may not deal with, or may deal with only under a licence.
steps.when: Every export, before you accept the order.
steps.chapterNote: Screen the end user as well as the distributor: seat parts and furniture components often ship to assembly plants in Canada and Mexico, and medical furniture to hospitals and health ministries abroad.

steps.title: Check whether you need an export licence
steps.whatToDo: Find the product's Export Control Classification Number (ECCN) on the Commerce Control List. Most goods are not listed and are EAR99. For a listed ECCN, look up the destination on the Commerce Country Chart under each reason for control: an X means a licence is needed unless a licence exception applies. Even EAR99 goods need a licence for embargoed countries and for restricted end users or end uses.
steps.when: Every export of goods subject to the Export Administration Regulations (EAR).
steps.chapterNote: Most furniture, mattresses, lighting and prefabricated buildings are EAR99. Aircraft seats (9401.10) can be parts specially designed for aircraft under ECCN 9A991.d, which is controlled for anti-terrorism reasons. For Russia and Belarus, Supplement No. 4 to Part 746 requires a licence for aircraft seats, motor-vehicle seats, wooden office furniture and prefabricated buildings even when they are EAR99.

steps.title: Check sanctions on the destination
steps.whatToDo: Check the destination against OFAC's sanctions programs and the EAR's embargo rules. Cuba, Iran and North Korea have country-wide rules, and Syria still needs a Commerce licence for most items; Russia and Belarus need a licence for any item with an ECCN. Several programs have special permissions for food and medicine.
steps.when: Exports to a sanctioned or embargoed country, or to a listed person anywhere.

steps.title: File the export in AES (Electronic Export Information)
steps.whatToDo: You (the U.S. principal party in interest) or your freight forwarder file the EEI in the Automated Export System — free through ACE AESDirect — and put the confirmation number (ITN) on the shipping documents. File at least 24 hours before an ocean shipment is loaded, 2 hours before a flight departs, or 1 hour before a truck reaches the border. Not filing can cost a civil penalty of up to $17,412 per violation.
steps.when: When one Schedule B number in one shipment to one buyer is worth over $2,500, and at any value when the shipment needs a Commerce licence or a DEA permit or declaration, or ships an EAR item to Cuba, Iran, North Korea or Syria, or a Commerce Control List item to China, Russia or Venezuela.
steps.chapterNote: Shipments to Canada, the largest buyer, are generally exempt from EEI filing unless they need a licence or another exception applies (15 CFR 30.36). For other destinations a container of furniture or seat parts is almost always worth more than $2,500 per Schedule B number, so plan to file in AES.

rules.title: Products that do not meet U.S. safety rules: a product that does not comply with a CPSC rule, such as a mattress that fails the federal flammability standards (16 CFR 1632 and 1633) or a dresser or other clothing storage unit that fails the tip-over standard (16 CFR 1261), can be exported only after the exporter files a statement with CPSC at least 30 days before export (16 CFR Part 1019); CPSC can object to the export. Products that meet U.S. rules need no notice.

Medical furniture: hospital beds, examination and operating tables, dentists' chairs and similar furniture are medical devices. A device legally marketed in the U.S. can be exported, and FDA issues a Certificate to Foreign Government (CFG) that many foreign regulators ask for; an unapproved device can be exported only under FD&C Act section 801(e) (meets the importing country's requirements, labeled for export) or section 802.

Russia and Belarus: Supplement No. 4 to Part 746 lists aircraft seats (9401.10), motor-vehicle seats (9401.20), wooden office furniture (9403.30) and prefabricated buildings (9406.10, 9406.20, 9406.90), so they need a BIS licence to Russia or Belarus even when they are EAR99 (15 CFR 746.8).

Aircraft seats: seats and seat parts specially designed for civil aircraft can be classified under ECCN 9A991.d (parts and components specially designed for aircraft), controlled for anti-terrorism reasons, so a licence is needed only for the destinations those controls cover; confirm the ECCN with the seat maker.

groups.label: Seats, chairs, sofas & parts
groups.note: Aircraft and motor-vehicle seats need a BIS licence for Russia and Belarus; aircraft seats may be ECCN 9A991.d.

groups.label: Medical, dental & barber furniture
groups.note: Hospital beds, examination tables and dentists' chairs are FDA-regulated devices; foreign buyers usually ask for a Certificate to Foreign Government.

groups.label: Office, kitchen, bedroom & other furniture
groups.note: Dressers and other clothing storage units must meet CPSC's tip-over standard (16 CFR 1261) to be sold in the U.S.; units that do not can be exported only after the 30-day CPSC notice. Wooden office furniture needs a licence for Russia and Belarus.

groups.label: Mattresses, pillows, quilts & sleeping bags
groups.note: Mattresses must meet 16 CFR 1632 and 1633 for U.S. sale; a non-compliant mattress needs the 30-day CPSC export notice.

groups.label: Lamps, luminaires, LED fixtures & illuminated signs
Prefabricated buildings
groups.note: Prefabricated buildings need a BIS licence for Russia and Belarus.

savings.title: Claim the free-trade-agreement rate abroad
savings.saves: The partner country's tariff on qualifying U.S. goods — often 0% instead of its normal rate.
savings.appliesTo: Goods that meet the agreement's rules of origin, shipped to one of the 20 U.S. free-trade-agreement partners: Australia, Bahrain, Canada, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Israel, Jordan, Korea, Mexico, Morocco, Nicaragua, Oman, Panama, Peru and Singapore.
savings.document: A certification of origin from the exporter, producer or importer, which the buyer uses to claim the rate at import. For USMCA there is no set form, but it must contain the nine data elements in Annex 5-A.
savings.caveat: Whoever certifies must be able to back it up: for USMCA, a U.S. exporter or producer keeps origin records for at least 5 years, gives CBP a copy on request and tells buyers promptly about errors. Check the product's rule of origin and the partner's rate in the FTA Tariff Tool first.

savings.title: Get U.S. duty back on imported inputs (drawback)
savings.saves: 99% of the U.S. import duties, taxes and fees paid on goods or materials that are exported, or used to make the goods you export.
savings.appliesTo: Imported goods exported unused, and imported materials used to make an exported product (or, under the substitution rules, goods of the same kind).
savings.document: An electronic drawback claim in ACE, filed within 5 years of the import date, with the import and export records that tie the two together.
savings.caveat: Antidumping and countervailing duties are not refunded, and CBP takes no paper claims. The refund is on U.S. duties only; it does not lower the buyer's tariff.

savings.title: Have your Canadian buyer claim remission of Canada's surtax
savings.saves: Canada's 25% or 50% surtax on listed U.S. seats, furniture and lighting, for buyers that use the goods in Canadian manufacturing or processing, and for health-care, public-safety and national-security buyers.
savings.appliesTo: U.S. Chapter 94 goods under the United States Surtax Order (2026) imported into Canada for those uses.
savings.document: The Canadian importer claims remission from the CBSA under the United States Surtax Remission Order (2025), which SOR/2026-186 extended to the 2026 surtax.
savings.caveat: Conditions and time limits apply, and goods sold as is to retailers or consumers do not qualify. The global Steel Derivative Goods Surtax has its own, separate remission order.

citations.label: United States Surtax Remission Order (2025), SOR/2025-122

savings.title: Have your Chinese buyer use China's tariff exclusion process
savings.saves: China's 2019 counter-tariffs answering U.S. Section 301, which apply to some U.S. Chapter 94 lines (for example 10% on swivel chairs, medical furniture and electric lamps in Annex 3) on top of the 10% extra tariff when the buyer holds no exclusion.
savings.appliesTo: U.S. furniture, seats, bedding and lighting imported into China by a buyer whose exclusion covers the goods.
savings.document: The Chinese importer applies on China's Ministry of Finance exclusion system; the U.S. exporter supplies product and origin details.
savings.caveat: Exclusions are valid until December 31, 2026 and no extension is announced. They do not remove China's extra 10% on all U.S. goods.
